metaDescription: Five corded SDS-Plus rotary hammers under $150 compared on impact energy in joules, amp draw, weight and what budget bits and clutches really deliver.
expertTake: A rotary hammer under $150 is a corded SDS-Plus tool that will drill anchor holes in concrete and chip a few tiles, and the two ENEACRO models are the pick of the group because they publish real impact energy and ship with a safety clutch. The 13-amp ENEACRO ENRH3201 is the best overall, the 12.5-amp ENEACRO is the value pick for concrete, and the Deshuo is the pick for ceiling work. Skip this tier if you will break up slabs or drill dozens of holes a day, because the motors and the cheap bits will not last.
introParagraphs: A rotary hammer is not a bigger hammer drill. It drives the bit with an internal piston that fires a heavy blow down the shank while the bit turns, which is why it can bore into concrete in seconds when a standard hammer drill would take minutes and overheat.

Budget versions make that mechanism affordable, but they also cut corners in places the spec sheet does not show. This guide explains what the numbers mean, which compromises are acceptable for an occasional homeowner and what to watch for before the first hole. The quick picks are above, and the reviews below match each tool to a job.

products.name: ENEACRO ENRH3201 1-1/4-Inch SDS-Plus Rotary Hammer, 13 Amp

specList.label: Functions
specList.value: Four modes including drill only and hammering

products.description:
The ENRH3201 is the strongest tool here on paper. A 13 amp motor is the biggest in the roundup, and its 5.5 foot-pounds of impact energy converts to roughly 7.5 joules, the highest figure of the group. Impact energy is the force of each piston blow, and it is the number that decides how quickly a carbide tip fractures the stone ahead of it.

It offers four functions, including drill only for wood and steel, while the 12.5 amp ENEACRO has three. A safety clutch disengages the drive if the bit binds in rebar, which spares your wrist. In practice the clutch is the most important feature on a budget hammer, because jamming in rebar is the commonest way to get hurt. Against the 12.5 amp ENEACRO with 7 joules it gives you one more mode and about half a joule more claimed energy.

The cost is a heavy, loud tool and a motor that will heat up under constant work. Give it a rest every few minutes in concrete and keep the vents clear. Replace the included bits with reputable carbide-tipped SDS-Plus bits when they dull, since cheap tips are the weakest link of the whole kit.
products.bestFor: Homeowners who need anchor holes and light chiseling and want the strongest tool in this tier.
pros: Highest impact energy claim in the roundup
Four modes against three on the other ENEACRO
Safety clutch protects against bit binding
13 amp motor is the largest in the group
cons: Heavy and loud for overhead work
Budget motor heats under continuous drilling
Supplied bits are weaker than quality carbide

products.name: ENEACRO 1-1/4-Inch SDS-Plus 12.5 Amp Rotary Hammer, 7J

specList.label: Functions
specList.value: Drill only, hammer drill, hammer only

products.description:
This ENEACRO states its impact energy in joules, 7 J or about 5.2 ft-lbs, and that clear unit makes it easier to trust than listings that bury the figure. The three functions cover the jobs a homeowner actually does: drilling wood and steel, hammer drilling in masonry and hammer-only chiseling. The adjustable side handle and vibration control reduce the numbness that builds up after the tenth hole.

The difference from the 13 amp model is modest. You give up about half a joule of claimed energy and a fourth mode, and in exchange you get a lower amp draw that is easier on a 15 amp household circuit shared with a vacuum or lights. In a dusty garage that circuit headroom matters. Against the WORKPRO at 7.5 amps, it hits noticeably harder and goes through concrete faster.

Ownership tips are simple. Keep the chuck clean and lightly greased, because SDS-Plus bits slide in a groove and dry grooves wear. Let the tool do the work and do not lean on it, since pushing hard on a budget piston mechanism heats it without drilling faster.
products.bestFor: Buyers who want near-top impact energy without the extra mode and weight.
pros: Publishes impact energy clearly in joules
Vibration control and adjustable side handle
Lower amp draw than the 13 amp model
Safety clutch protects against binding
cons: Only three functions against the 13 amp's four
Heavy compared with the lightest options

products.name: DEKOPRO 1-1/4-Inch SDS-Plus Rotary Hammer, 12.5 Amp, 5.5J
products.description:
The DEKOPRO matches the ENEACRO's 12.5 amp motor but claims 5.5 joules, a full 1.5 joules less than the ENEACRO's 7 J. That gap is real: a stronger blow fractures concrete more quickly, so the DEKOPRO will take longer per hole at the same bit size. Its 0-4,600 blows per minute is lower than the Deshuo's 5,300, trading blow frequency for blow weight.

A side multifunction selector switches among four modes, and a safety clutch is fitted, which matches the more expensive ENEACRO models. The 12.5 amp motor draws a lot of current, so use a short, thick extension cord if you need one. A light cord drops voltage and starves the motor.

It makes sense as a middle choice: more energy than the Deshuo, less than the ENEACRO. For a few anchor holes in a basement wall, that is plenty. Check that bits seat with a firm click, and pull on them to confirm they are locked, since a loose SDS bit in a hammering tool can walk.
products.bestFor: Occasional users who want four modes and a safety clutch in a mid-strength tool.
pros: Four modes with a side selector
Safety clutch included
5.5 J is enough for anchor holes in concrete
Clear blows-per-minute figure
cons: 1.5 J less impact energy than the ENEACRO 12.5
Draws 12.5 amps, which taxes a shared circuit
Weaker brand support than established names

products.name: WORKPRO 1-1/4-Inch SDS-Plus Rotary Hammer, 7.5 Amp, 5 Bits

specList.label: Functions
specList.value: Hammer drill, hammer, drill, chisel adjust

specList.label: Durability claim
specList.value: Passes a one-meter drop test (maker claim)

products.description:
The WORKPRO is the lightest-powered tool in the group at 7.5 amps, which shows what a smaller motor means: it does not state impact energy on the listing, and the lower amp draw implies less blow energy than the 12.5 and 13 amp models. It is aimed at lighter demolition chipping and small anchor holes. The kit includes five SDS-Plus bits, so you can start without a separate purchase.

The four functions include a chisel-adjust mode and a 360-degree rotatable handle, which lets you grip it in awkward positions. The drop-test claim is a manufacturer statement and not an independent rating. Compared with the ENEACRO 12.5, it is a gentler tool that will take longer to cut concrete, though it also draws a lot less current and runs cooler.

The bits in a bundle are usually adequate for a handful of holes, but plan to replace them with better carbide if you drill often. Check the drive end for a clean groove and keep it greased. For a first rotary hammer where most of your work is tile removal and light concrete, this is a reasonable, modest choice.
products.bestFor: Light chipping and small anchors where a kit of bits matters more than raw power.
pros: Includes five SDS-Plus bits to start
Four modes including chisel adjust
Rotatable handle for awkward grips
Lower amp draw runs on any circuit
cons: Does not state impact energy on the listing
Weaker blow than the 12.5 and 13 amp tools
Slower in concrete than the ENEACRO models

products.name: Deshuo 1-Inch SDS-Plus Rotary Hammer, 9 Amp, 7.2 lb
products.description:
The Deshuo is the lightest tool at 7.19 pounds, a significant advantage when you are holding it overhead or drilling downward for long periods. Its impact energy is 3 joules, or about 2.2 foot-pounds, less than half the ENEACRO 12.5's 7 joules. The high blow rate of 0-5,300 per minute compensates partly by striking more often, but each strike is lighter.

It is a tool for small masonry holes, mortar joints and light chipping, not for big concrete. The listing is clear that it works only with SDS-Plus bits, not standard drill bits or SDS-Max, which is a good warning for first-time buyers who assume any hammer drill accepts any bit. A 1-inch rated capacity is realistic for a tool of this size.

For a homeowner mounting shelves on a brick wall or drilling a few holes in a block foundation, the Deshuo is enough. Do not buy it to run a 1-inch core bit through reinforced concrete, since the lower impact energy will leave you waiting. Wear hearing protection and a dust mask, because masonry dust is a respiratory hazard.
products.bestFor: Overhead drilling, small masonry holes and users who need a light tool.
pros: Lightest in the group at 7.19 lb
Highest blow rate at 5,300 BPM
Easier on the wrist overhead
Clear warning about bit compatibility
cons: 3 J impact energy is less than half the ENEACRO's
Too light for larger concrete work

buyingCriteria.explanation: Impact energy is the force of each piston blow and the best single predictor of speed in concrete. The ENEACRO 12.5 claims 7 J, the 13 amp ENEACRO about 7.5 J, the DEKOPRO 5.5 J and the Deshuo 3 J. Less than 3 J is a light-duty tool, and 5 J or more begins to handle real anchor work. Avoid comparing amps alone, since a poorly built motor draws high current and delivers little. As a rule of thumb, under 3 J is for mortar joints and brick, 3 to 5 J for light concrete anchors, and 5 J and above for repeated anchor holes in cured concrete.

Listings mix joules and foot-pounds, and one foot-pound equals about 1.36 joules. The ENEACRO 13 amp's 5.5 ft-lbs is about 7.5 J, while the DEKOPRO's 5.5 J is only about 4 ft-lbs. They look identical on the page but differ by roughly a third. Convert to joules before comparing. When a listing says 1-1/4 inch capacity, that refers to the largest bit the mechanism is rated to turn, not a size it will drill quickly.

SDS-Plus bits have two open grooves that let the bit slide a few millimeters while the hammer strikes it, so the full blow reaches the tip. They do not fit standard chucks and do not fit SDS-Max tools. Buy quality carbide-tipped bits, since a cheap bit transfers less energy and chips at the tip. Reputable carbide bits from established makers cost a fraction of the tool but make a large difference to speed, so budget for two or three.

When a bit jams in rebar, a rotary hammer wants to spin the whole tool in your hands. A clutch slips and cuts the drive. The ENEACRO and DEKOPRO models include one and the Deshuo and WORKPRO listings we reviewed do not mention one, which makes it a deciding factor. Never run a hammer without the side handle. The clutch is the most important safety feature, and a tool without one can twist hard enough to sprain a wrist when a bit binds in rebar.

The Deshuo weighs 7.19 pounds and the heavier tools weigh more, which matters when drilling ceilings. Heavy tools hammer better downward, because gravity adds force, but become exhausting overhead. Choose by the direction of most of your holes. If most of your holes are in a ceiling, the Deshuo's lower weight is worth more than the ENEACRO's extra joules.

A 13 amp tool on a 15 amp circuit leaves little headroom, and a thin extension cord starves the motor. Use a heavy 12-gauge cord under 50 feet and avoid sharing the circuit with a vacuum. The WORKPRO at 7.5 amps and Deshuo at 9 amps are far gentler on the circuit. Run the tool on a dedicated outlet if you can, because a 12.5 or 13 amp tool will trip a shared 15 amp breaker.

specDecoder.meaning: A joule is the energy of each hammer blow. More joules mean each strike fractures more stone, so the bit advances faster. For comparison, a standard hammer drill delivers well under 1 joule per blow, so even the Deshuo's 3 J is several times stronger.
specDecoder.watchFor: Some budget listings omit joules or quote foot-pounds. The WORKPRO states neither.

specDecoder.meaning: BPM counts hammer blows per minute. A higher rate is smoother but each blow is usually lighter. A 7 J blow is closer to what small professional SDS-Plus tools deliver, but budget tools may not sustain it for long.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Deshuo's 5,300 BPM looks big but its blows are only 3 J. Do not rank by BPM.

specDecoder.meaning: Amps measure current draw, a proxy for motor size. A larger motor can sustain more load without overheating. Amps also tell you what size of cord and breaker you need.
specDecoder.watchFor: Amps do not equal power at the bit. Poor mechanisms waste current as heat.

specDecoder.meaning: The listed 1 inch or 1-1/4 inch is the maximum hole size in concrete with a core bit. Hole size in concrete should be matched to the bit, and larger holes need a drilling pause to clear dust.
specDecoder.watchFor: Do not expect to drill 1-1/4 inch holes quickly in a budget tool. Real use is 1/4 to 5/8 inch.

specDecoder.meaning: Modes are drill only, hammer drill, hammer only for chiseling and sometimes chisel positioning. Chisel modes lock the bit so it does not rotate, which is a different function from hammer drilling.
specDecoder.watchFor: Check that hammer only is listed if you plan to chisel tile.

howWeEvaluated.title: Impact energy first
howWeEvaluated.description: We ranked tools by claimed impact energy, converting units where needed. The ENEACRO 13 amp (about 7.5 J), the ENEACRO 12.5 amp (7 J), the DEKOPRO (5.5 J) and the Deshuo (3 J) form the ladder. We read units carefully because listings mix joules and foot-pounds, and converting them changed the ranking between the DEKOPRO and ENEACRO.

howWeEvaluated.title: Protection features
howWeEvaluated.description: We gave credit for a safety clutch, side handle and vibration control, because these prevent injuries on tools that bind in rebar. We noted which listings mention a clutch, vibration control or a side handle and did not assume any.

howWeEvaluated.title: Weight and handling
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared weight, since the Deshuo's 7.19 pounds is a real advantage for overhead use. Weight was weighed against impact energy, so the Deshuo earned credit for being 7.19 pounds even with lower energy.

howWeEvaluated.title: Kit and bits
howWeEvaluated.description: We noted what comes in the box, such as the WORKPRO's five bits, and the compatibility warning on the Deshuo listing. We counted included bits as a small plus, since a kit lets a first-time buyer start immediately.

howWeEvaluated.title: Fit across the lineup
howWeEvaluated.description: Each tool was placed by job, from tile chipping to anchor holes. We assumed an occasional homeowner user, which means anchor holes, mortar and light tile chipping.

howToChoose.note: For slabs or demolition, buy a full-size SDS-Max tool, not any of these.

cards.label: Light
cards.text: The Deshuo at 7.19 pounds and 3 J, and the WORKPRO at 7.5 amps, are easier to hold but slower in concrete.

cards.label: Heavy

Always use the side handle and eye and ear protection.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: At least 5 J of impact energy, a clutch and a depth stop. Use a 3/16 to 1/4 inch carbide bit for anchors.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The ENEACRO 13 amp and 12.5 amp are best, with the DEKOPRO close behind. The Deshuo works for mortar joints.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You drill dozens of holes weekly or use core bits. The ENEACRO 13 amp is the ceiling here.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You need a few holes a year. The Deshuo or WORKPRO is enough.

maintenance.why: SDS grooves need grease to slide. Dry grooves wear quickly. Always unplug before changing bits.
Masonry dust clogs vents and overheats the motor. Light lubricant on the bit shank extends bit life.
Chipped carbide tips reduce speed. Replace them. Replace worn carbon brushes if the tool stutters.
Damaged cords are a shock hazard. Replace them. Check the side handle clamp is tight.

maintenance.interval: Every few minutes of heavy use
maintenance.why: Budget motors overheat. Short breaks extend life. Keep it dry, since concrete dust draws moisture.

faq.q: Is a rotary hammer better than a hammer drill?
faq.a: For concrete, yes. A piston mechanism gives much heavier blows. A hammer drill is a clutch that taps and is much weaker. Wear safety glasses and hearing protection, and use a dust mask when drilling concrete.

faq.q: Can I use SDS-Plus bits in a regular drill?
faq.a: No. They need an SDS-Plus chuck. Also standard round bits do not work well in a rotary hammer. Let the tool's weight and hammer do the work, and avoid leaning hard on it.

faq.q: What size anchors can I drill?
faq.a: These tools suit 1/4 to 5/8 inch holes. Larger sizes are slow and need heavier tools. Clear the dust from the hole by withdrawing the bit while it runs, then set the anchor.
For a few holes, yes. For regular work buy carbide-tipped bits from a known brand, since cheap tips chip. A corded rotary hammer will outlast a cheap cordless one for repeated concrete work.
Yes. A rotary hammer is loud and prolonged exposure can damage hearing.
No. They can bind in rebar, so a clutch is vital. Use a carbide bit and stop if it hits metal.
